sections.text:
Robot swarms harness simple, local interactions among many individually limited robots to produce complex, coordinated collective behavior, making them valuable across domains from agriculture to disaster response. We envision the next frontier for such swarms as open swarms, in which robots join or leave the swarm dynamically at runtime.

The ability to dynamically adjust swarm size has been shown to be beneficial, for instance by reducing inconsistencies and network partitioning, especially under sparse connectivity or in complex environments, ultimately improving task performance.

For practical deployment, however, open swarms requires governance, particularly protection against Byzantine behavior (i.e., faulty or malicious robots), since allowing robots to join freely also makes the swarm easier to infiltrate.

Blockchain technology has recently been incorporated into robot swarms, offering secure, decentralized coordination and improved resilience, though largely in closed settings with a fixed, predetermined membership.

In this work, we extend these benefits to open swarms by introducing robot swarms governed by a blockchain-based decentralized autonomous organization (DAO), in which the swarm regulates itself using autonomous rules encoded in smart contracts.

We outline several DAO-based governance mechanisms for robot swarms, depending on the needs of the application, and present a proof-of-concept implementation of a simple DAO that regulates swarm membership and prevents Byzantine infiltration.

Our simulation results and real-robot validations show that DAO-governed access control and robot removal can maintain proper swarm functioning while keeping the number of Byzantine robots within acceptable limits.

items.title: Self-governed access control in open robot swarms using a blockchain-based DAO

Automotive radar is a key sensing modality for safety-critical vehicle functions due to its robustness under adverse weather and lighting conditions. Recent advances in AI-based radar perception enable the direct estimation of object parameters from a single radar measurement cycle.

However, the internal decision process of data-driven models is typically not explicitly linked to the underlying radar sensing physics. Consequently, object estimates may achieve high statistical accuracy while remaining physically inconsistent with the measured radar signature, particularly in previously unseen scenarios.

Such inconsistencies are especially critical for heading estimation, as they directly affect trajectory prediction and collision assessment in pre-crash scenarios. This paper presents a physics-based consistency assessment framework for validating AI-derived vehicle hypotheses in automotive radar perception.

The proposed approach generates an expected radar signature from AI-estimated object parameters using a physics-based reference model that incorporates occlusion-dependent edge visibility, aspect- and angle-dependent RCS modeling, and characteristic wheel-induced MD signatures.

The expected signature is compared with the observed radar point cloud using a Wasserstein-distance-based consistency metric computed from three complementary features: the spatial distribution of detections along object edges, the local detection count, and the radar reflection intensity.

In this way, physically implausible object hypotheses can be identified and corrected independently of the underlying neural network architecture and without model retraining or architectural modifications. The proposed consistency module is integrated as a cascaded post-processing stage for vehicle heading estimation.

items.title: Physics-Based Plausibility Assessment of AI-Predicted Vehicle Parameters for Automotive Radar in Pre-Crash Scenarios

Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution.

An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state.

An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands.

The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. sections.text:
Multicopters are a type of aerial robot seeing extensive real-world applications but with range and endurance as critical bottlenecks. Optimization of its energy efficiency through energy-aware flight planning (e.g. cruise speed-scheduling) has hence been an important topic.

The mass of the multicopter is an important factor to consider, as it has a significant impact on efficiency, and many common applications are subject to frequent mass variation due to payload change.

This work derives closed-form scaling relationships between the energy-optimal steady horizontal flight behavior of a multicopter and its vehicle mass, and validates them experimentally on two multirotor platforms.

Specifically, for mass-only variation, i.e., when payload changes the vehicle mass while the airframe geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and rotor configuration remain unchanged, we show through a combination of numerical simulation, theoretical derivation, and experimental validation that （1） the energy-optimal velocity is proportional to the square root of vehicle mass; （2） the energy-optimal pitch angle is constant with respect to mass; and （3） the optimal energy per meter is proportional to mass.

The analysis shows that these three relationships arise from a common mass-similarity property of the steady-state flight and rotor-aerodynamic equations. Furthermore, the obtained scaling relationships enable simple yet effective cruise-speed planning to optimize energy efficiency and extend the range and endurance of the multicopter.

items.title: Mass Scaling Laws for Energy-Optimal Horizontal Multirotor Flight

Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout.

However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation.

RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low.

At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors.

Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

A dexterous hand succeeds or fails through contact, yet every scalable record of human manipulation (video, vision-based hand tracking, motion capture) observes how the hand moves and misses how it pushes.

We present DexCanvas, a hybrid real-synthetic dataset of 7,000 hours of dexterous hand-object interaction with per-frame contact points and contact forces, grown from 70 hours of optical motion capture that spans 21 manipulation types, from power and precision grasps to in-hand manipulation.

The forces come from a real-to-sim pipeline: one reinforcement learning (RL) policy, conditioned on object geometry and manipulation type, drives an actuated MANO hand in physics simulation to reproduce each captured object trajectory, and the simulator measures the contacts that produce the reproduced motion.

The policy reproduces 87.5% of the demonstrations and still succeeds on 80.9% of rollouts from perturbed initial object poses; these perturbed rollouts expand the 70 captured hours a hundredfold. On six YCB objects absent from the capture set it succeeds 72.5% of the time.

Reconstructing interactive, simulation-ready 3D scenes from a single image is a critical bottleneck for robotic manipulation. While recent single-image lifters recover plausible per-object shapes, composing them yields scenes that collapse under physical simulation due to interpenetrating, hovering, or sinking objects.

Existing physics-aware compositional reconstruction methods mainly address this as a post-hoc layout correction, leaving the underlying geometric errors unresolved. To address this, we introduce SimuScene, a compositional 3D reconstruction pipeline that puts physics in the loop of shape and layout estimation.

Rather than using physics merely for layout cleanup, we utilize the physics engine as a diagnostic measurement tool during the generative process itself.

By diagnostically simulating reconstructed objects under gravity, we convert penetration and support failures into quantitative correction signals that drive amodal shape resampling, with gravity-axis stretching as a lightweight correction for minor errors.

This physics-informed feedback loop mitigates accumulated reconstruction errors and produces a stable, simulation-ready compositional 3D scene. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on physical stability and geometric alignment benchmarks.

We further highlight SimuScene's utility by deploying reconstructed environments in humanoid control and robot-arm manipulation tasks.

Robotics and AI systems are increasingly deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) to follow high-level instructions, from routine household chores to more complex organizational tasks.

Yet, broad directives like "clean the room" or "organize the desk" frequently omit crucial details about user preferences and specific arrangement of objects that influence the desired outcome.

Without any further guidance, such models tend to overestimate their grasp of ambiguous instructions and frequently assume they have sufficient understanding despite missing important details.

In this paper, we propose CLARA (Conversational cLArification for Robotic Arrangement), a cognitively-driven clarification framework that proactively elicits key information from users, in a similar fashion as humans' clarification seeking behavior.

Through targeted questioning, CLARA refines ambiguous requests into structured, detailed instructions describing precisely how objects should be organized or rearranged, according to the user's preferences. These clarifications then guide a diffusion-based image generation pipeline, producing realistic visual renderings of the final, desired scene.

This final rendering also serves as a visual confirmation of the system's understanding from the user.

Experimental results and user studies demonstrate that CLARA leads to more accurate and consistent outcomes compared to another State-of-the-Art LVLM system, highlighting the importance of interactive clarification for bridging the gap between vague directives and fully grounded task specifications.

The advent of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) offers a promising technology to tackle the limitations of modular design in autonomous driving, which often falters in open-world scenarios requiring sustained environmental understanding and logical reasoning.

Besides, embodied artificial intelligence facilitates policy optimization through closed-loop interactions to achieve the continuous learning capability, thereby advancing autonomous driving toward embodied intelligent (EI) driving. However, such capability will be constrained by relying solely on LMMs to enhance EI driving without joint decision-making.

This article proposes a novel semantics and policy dual-driven hybrid decision framework to tackle this challenge, ensuring continuous learning and joint decision. The framework merges LMMs for semantic understanding and cognitive representation, and deep reinforcement learning for real-time policy optimization.

This article particularly details the foundational principles of EI driving and LMMs, and also introduces the emerging opportunities this framework enables, encompassing potential benefits and representative use cases.

The proposed framework, evaluated through a lane-change planning case study, achieves at least a 19% performance improvement over the baselines, as verified by simulations. Finally, key open challenges and future research directions are identified to guide subsequent work.

sections.text:
Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments.

Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK.

It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions.

Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2{\deg} on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%.

When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success.

These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.

sections.text:
A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts.

We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms.

To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence.

To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations.

We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator.

By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation.

PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not.

Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

items.title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations

In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting co-present others' access to or interpretation of that information. Publicly observable speech and gestures may not adequately support such exchanges.

We investigate a wearable-mediated channel for discreet interaction that combines in-ear audio messages with deliberate rightward head tilts as responses.

To examine its feasibility and participants' experiences, we studied 20 pairs (40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based conversational agent representing a social robot, controlled by a researcher in a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Each pair played with and without the channel.

One participant wore the device (the wearer), while the other (the non-wearer) was informed about the channel after gameplay. The channel conveyed information that could help the wearer or robot character select an opponent they could defeat. The information exchange and subsequent opponent selection occurred as intended in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns.

Wearers reported low perceived pressure/tension in both conditions, with no statistically significant difference between conditions, and favorable usability immediately after use. Retrospective interviews, however, revealed varied accounts of noticing the interaction among non-wearers and contrasting perceptions of teamwork and unfairness.

These findings support the feasibility of wearable-mediated exchanges within this game and identify awareness and fairness as considerations for future designs.

items.title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting

sections.text:
Modern GPUs and software frameworks have made sampling-based methods, such as reinforcement learning and model predictive path integral control, increasingly popular in robotics. However, the logic these methods can execute per sample is limited to what has been implemented on the GPU.

Nonlinear programs (NLPs) are one of the most expressive tools in robotics, reliably minimizing a cost while exactly enforcing general constraints. NLP optimizers were among the field's main workhorses, but were not designed for modern GPU hardware.

Embedding NLPs such as trajectory optimization and inverse kinematics directly within each sample would be highly valuable, yet the only current option is to call a CPU solver per sample, possibly in parallel on a multi-core CPU.

This bottlenecks the CPU, requires GPU-to-CPU-to-GPU transfers when the rest of the pipeline resides on the GPU, and leaves the GPU intermittently idle. To address this issue, in this work we present jaxipm, the first GPU-batched solver for generally constrained nonlinear optimization problems.

Our approach is a JAX implementation of the battle-tested IPOPT algorithm, facilitated by eliminating control flow through heterogeneous iteration fusion, and minimizing GPU idle time through iteration-level batching. Our implementation enables solving hundreds of NLPs in parallel on a single GPU.

We validate jaxipm on a range of quadrotor nonlinear model predictive control benchmarks, where on a single GPU we achieve between 30.7% and 69.9% of the throughput of 64 IPOPT instances running in parallel on a 64-core CPU. open-source codebase: https://github.com/johnviljoen/jaxipm

items.title: Scaling Nonlinear Optimization: Many Problems One GPU

World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction.

Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation.

The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder.

Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone.

Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.

sections.text:
Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels.

This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model.

In this paper, we present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that takes a standard model in .tflite or .safetensors format and emits all C source files needed for deployment: the inference engine (kernels, weight arrays, memory layout) and the RTOS integration layer with zero runtime dependencies.

On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms MCUNet TinyEngine by using 38% less SRAM (up to 5.9$\times$) and 15% less Flash, while generating complete C code rather than linking a pre-written kernel library. To demonstrate, we use te-comp to compile an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo transformer (TinyStories-v2) and deploy it on a single-core Cortex-M7 at 160MHz.

The full firmware uses 249KB of 512KB SRAM and 3.62MB of 4MB Flash and achieves approximately 1 token/s interactive text generation via Q4_0 weight quantization, a stateful int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning -- a capability no existing MCU inference framework supports.

items.title: te-comp: A Complete MLIR Compiler Generating Self-Contained C Inference Engines for MCUs

Social robots must coordinate speech and movement while interpreting multimodal human input. We present a multimodal framework that integrates speech, vision, and touch to generate contextually appropriate robot speech and movement.

We evaluated the framework in virtual reality with 18 participants across five social interaction scenarios, comparing its performance against a human-teleoperated baseline.

Although participants rated the autonomous system above the neutral midpoint for both naturalness and social appropriateness, the teleoperated baseline received significantly higher ratings on both measures.

Behavioral coding and qualitative feedback revealed that conversational timing, clarification of ambiguous requests, and spatial coordination were important factors contributing to this performance gap. These findings highlight key challenges in developing autonomous robots capable of natural, multimodal social interaction.

items.title: Multimodal Socially Aware Framework for Human-Robot Interaction in Virtual Reality

sections.text:
With the rapid advancement of underwater net-working and multi-agent coordination technologies, autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) ad-hoc networks have emerged as a pivotal framework for executing complex maritime missions, such as multi-target tracking.

However, traditional data-centricarchitectures struggle to maintain operational consistency under highly dynamic topological fluctuations and severely constrained acoustic communication bandwidth.

This article proposes a scene-adaptive embodied intelligence (EI) architecture for multi-AUV ad-hoc networks, which re-envisions AUVs as embodied entities by integrating perception, decision-making, and physical execution into a unified cognitive loop.

To materialize the functional interaction between these layers, we define a beacon-based communication and control model that treats the communication link as a dynamic constraint-aware channel, effectively bridging the gap between high-level policy inference and decentralized physical actuation.

Specifically, the proposed architecture employs a three-layer functional framework and introduces a Scene-Adaptive MARL (SA-MARL) algorithm featuring a dual-path critic mechanism.

By integrating a scene critic network and a general critic network through a weight-based dynamic fusion process, SA-MARL effectively decouples specialized tracking tasks from global safety constraints, facilitating autonomous policy evolution.

Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposedscheme significantly accelerates policy convergence and achieves superior tracking accuracy compared to mainstream MARL approaches, maintaining robust performance even under intense environmental interference and fluid topological shifts.

items.title: Multi-AUV Ad-hoc Networks-Based Multi-Target Tracking Based on Scene-Adaptive Embodied Intelligence

sections.text:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit semantic capabilities from pretrained VLMs, yet large-scale post-training on robot data and architectural modifications can reshape the backbone so extensively that it becomes difficult to isolate what the VLM contributes to control.

Directly converting pretrained VLMs into VLAs with minimal architectural change offers a more transparent path to understanding how VLM capabilities transfer across model scales.

The core obstacle is output-distribution mismatch: predicting actions as bare numeric token sequences moves generation away from the VLM's pretrained language distribution, degrading the capabilities we seek to preserve.

To address this, we propose CLAP (Causal Language-Action Prediction), which prepends each numeric action sequence with a natural-language action description, causally conditioning precise action-token prediction on a language-action plan without modifying the backbone architecture.

With only 4-5 hours of training, 2B CLAP achieves 90.8% on LIBERO (+14.9 pt over VLA-0) and improves robustness on LIBERO-PRO under language, object, and spatial perturbations. Ablations attribute the gains to action-grounded language semantics, and on a real UR5e robot 2B CLAP reaches 60% success against 15% for matched VLA-0.

We release CLAP at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B as an open-weight, multi-scale compact VLA family from a single VLM lineage, enabling controlled analysis of VLM-to-VLA capability transfer.

items.title: CLAP: Direct VLM-to-VLA Adaptation via Language-Action Grounding

sections.text:
In robotics, shape control, or shape servoing, refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object toward a desired shape. This article is the second of a two-part tutorial on data-driven, Jacobian-based shape control, in which the deformation Jacobian, a local model of how robot motion changes the measured shape, is estimated from measurements.

Part I built the shape-servoing loop and derived a local stability condition. This paper starts by using the singular value decomposition of the deformation Jacobian to identify shape changes that can be produced by small robot motions, those that require large robot motions, and those that are locally unavailable.

It then analyses how the choice of shape features determines how the controller regulates the object's shape and, therefore, how much the object deforms on its way to the target. It then describes three ways in which the shape control loop can fail: loss of controllability, loss of observability, and occurrence of mechanical instabilities.

It closes with shape-control extensions to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.

items.title: A Tutorial on Shape Servoing of Deformable Objects-Part II: Advanced Concepts

sections.text:
Teleoperation of mobile robots in communication-denied environments requires maintaining a communication link while allowing the operator to maneuver freely. We propose a shared-autonomy framework in which a teleoperated leader is followed by a chain of autonomous robots that relays a line of sight to a fixed base station, a geometric proxy for the link.

Connectivity is enforced geometrically through visibility-based Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), with each agent computing its control input locally through a quadratic program. A strict visibility constraint guarantees connectivity, but a follower with no independent motion objective remains stationary, stalling the leader at the boundary of the safe set.

Relaxing it preserves mobility at the cost of the guarantee.

Our framework resolves this conflict through nested hard-soft visibility constraints: a full field-of-view (FoV) constraint enforced strictly to guarantee connectivity and a contracted FoV constraint imposed on each follower as a relaxed behavioral objective that drives it inward before the connectivity boundary is reached.

We prove feasibility of the local quadratic programs and forward invariance of the connected, collision-free set under the resulting distributed controller. The contraction parameter shapes follower behavior without affecting the guarantee, which follows from the strict constraint alone.

The framework is evaluated in confined and cluttered environments on two simulated systems: a kinematic integrator and software-in-the-loop Crazyflie quadrotors. Compared with a baseline tuned to reach the goal in comparable time, the framework keeps the links far closer to the connected set and moves the followers less.

items.title: Nested Field-of-View Barriers for Teleoperated Multi-Robot Relay Chains

Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions.

We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations.

On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves $75.0\%$ out-of-distribution success, compared with $27.9\%$ for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches $70.0\%$ mean success, compared with $36.0\%$ for the strongest baseline.

RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers.

A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.

items.title: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training

sections.text:
AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present.

From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded.

Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time.

The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR.

We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io.

Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.

items.title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data

sections.text:
Humanoid locomotion requires deciding where to step and how to distribute contact forces. However, a disturbance can invalidate the nominal plan, requiring coordinated revision under constraints that switch with every footfall.

To solve this online, the proposed approach employs the single-rigid-body model, which retains attitude dynamics and the full contact wrench. An iterative linear-quadratic-regulator MPC (iLQR-MPC) then jointly optimizes contact forces and footstep locations in a single receding-horizon problem, without a separate step planner.

Specifically, contact and motion constraints are incorporated into the backward pass through augmented-Lagrangian and relaxed-barrier penalties. A whole-body controller subsequently maps the plan to joint torques at 500 Hz while preserving contact feasibility.

The model-based formulation makes disturbance responses interpretable through explicit costs and constraints, and requires no platform-specific policy training. In MuJoCo simulations, the iLQR-MPC replans at 100 Hz (mean solve time 8.9 ms); the Unitree G1 sustains steady-state walking and recovers from impulsive 245 N forward and 175 N lateral pushes.

items.title: Online iLQR-MPC with Whole-Body Control for Robust Humanoid Locomotion

sections.text:
Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity.

Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility.

To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies.

In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency.

Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes.

On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments.

Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline.

These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.

sections.text:
Dexterous manipulation involves not only moving objects, but also arranging the hand around them to maintain useful contacts and enable subsequent actions. Yet many learning-based systems specify goals primarily through object poses or trajectories, leaving hand-object configurations to emerge implicitly.

We introduce DexHOT, which formulates dexterous manipulation as hand-object configuration transfer: moving between feasible configurations that jointly specify hand articulation and object pose relative to the wrist.

DexHOT learns a reusable relation-conditioned transfer primitive from synthetic feasible configuration pairs, without human reference motions, and composes long-horizon behaviors through closed-loop tracking of configuration subgoals.

On DexHOTBench with 120 objects, a single policy achieves 80.5% transfer success on seen objects and 69.4% on unseen objects; on a real dexterous hand, it achieves 61.5% success over 200 real-robot transfers and 90% task success across six demonstration-guided tasks.

These results show that explicit hand-object goals provide an expressive and composable interface for dexterous manipulation. More details and videos are available at https://dex-hot.github.io/.

items.title: DexHOT: Learning Hand-Object Configuration Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation

Coordinating autonomous underwater vehicles requires translating operator intent into feasible assignments while preserving autonomous execution when communication is limited.

We present a hierarchical framework that couples Large Language Model (LLM) interpretation of natural-language mission instructions with Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) and distributed Behaviour Tree (BT) execution.

The LLM extracts assignment and ordering constraints, which the MILP optimizer combines with vehicle capabilities and temporal requirements. A BT-LLM Bridge distributes the resulting allocations to onboard BT Mission Managers.

Per-vehicle Robotic Agents assess local faults and request selective replanning, allowing unaffected vehicles to continue their assigned tasks. Evaluation in a ROS-based AUV simulator compares Qwen-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B on constraint extraction and tests recovery from sensor degradation and critical vehicle faults.

Qwen-3-8B provides more accurate constraint extraction, and all tasks are completed in the tested failure scenarios. These simulation results support the feasibility of combining language-based mission specification with structured allocation and distributed execution.

sections.text:
The integration of quantum computing into robotics requires mathematical representations that preserve the geometric structure and configuration dependence of robot motion.

This paper introduces a structure-preserving quantum representation of rigid-body transformations and serial-manipulator kinematics, establishing a correspondence between classical kinematic models and parameterized quantum circuits.

Building on the Bloch-sphere representation, spatial directions are encoded into single-qubit states, while quantum rotations reproduce the ordered composition of reference-frame transformations.

Translational contributions are combined through quantum-state aggregation, with their metric scales retained classically, enabling the reconstruction of end-effector position and orientation from Pauli expectation values. The formulation preserves the original joint variables and accommodates different kinematic conventions and joint types.

Beyond forward kinematics, we establish that the manipulator geometric Jacobian can be reconstructed from quantum-observable derivatives using the parameter-shift rule, with analytical equivalence to its classical counterpart under ideal readout.

To demonstrate the applicability of this representation to robot-level algorithms, we introduce Quantum Closed Loop Inverse Kinematics, a hybrid closed-loop method that exploits quantum-derived pose and Jacobian information.

The proposed framework provides a geometrically interpretable foundation for developing and investigating quantum and hybrid computational methods for robotic kinematics and motion.

summary.en: The paper introduces a structure-preserving quantum representation of rigid-body transformations and serial-manipulator kinematics using parameterized circuits. It encodes spatial directions in single-qubit states, models ordered frame rotations, and aggregates translations while retaining metric scales classically. The authors state that end-effector pose can be reconstructed from Pauli expectations and that the geometric Jacobian can be recovered from observable derivatives using the parameter-shift rule, with analytical equivalence to the classical Jacobian under ideal readout. They also introduce a hybrid closed-loop inverse-kinematics method.

sections.text:
Fast quadrupedal navigation requires preparing for the next turn while approaching the current goal. Policies trained to reach and remain at a single target can instead produce stop-and-go motion when applied to sequential goals, compromising its agility potential.

We introduce PrepTurn, a reinforcement learning framework for anticipatory maneuvering in sequential local navigation. PrepTurn maps the current and next pose goals directly to joint actions, using the upcoming goal to inform how the robot should approaches the current one.

Its persistent-credit reward encourages timely completion of the whole sequence by continuing to reward reached goals while moving on and preparing subsequent maneuvers, and an automatic curriculum that gradually increases goal difficulty is critical for learning stable turning behaviors.

Together, these components enable the policy to coordinate approach speed and reorientation across goal transitions without prescribed trajectories or arrival times. Simulation and onboard Unitree Go2 experiments demonstrate fast, efficient sequential traversal with high completion and reduced stop-and-go motion.

We further show that when the goal-reaching tolerances are more relaxed, the policy learns to exploit the freedom allowed by the task with emergent behaviors, such as turning to the next goal in advance and cutting corners within the permitted regions behaviors, to traverse goal sequences more efficiently.

summary.en: The paper introduces PrepTurn, a reinforcement learning framework that maps current and next pose goals directly to quadruped joint actions, allowing the upcoming goal to shape the approach to the current one. Persistent-credit rewards and an automatic difficulty curriculum support sequence-level maneuvering without prescribed trajectories or arrival times. The authors report fast, efficient traversal with less stop-and-go motion in simulation and onboard Unitree Go2 experiments. With relaxed goal tolerances, the policy also exhibits behaviors such as turning early and cutting corners within permitted regions.
summary.zh: 论文提出 PrepTurn 强化学习框架，使四足机器人依据当前和下一目标姿态生成关节动作，以提前准备转向。其持续信用奖励鼓励机器人完成整段目标序列，自动课程逐步提高目标难度。作者称，该方法无需预设轨迹或到达时间，即可协调接近速度与转向；仿真和 Unitree Go2 机载实验显示其能快速、高效地连续通过目标，并减少走走停停。目标容差放宽时，策略还会提前转向、在允许区域内切角。

sections.text:
The pursuit of general-purpose robotic manipulation is hindered by the scarcity of diverse, real-world interaction data. Unlike large-scale web vision-language data, robotic data collection incurs prohibitive physical costs.

The key challenge is thus not merely to collect more robot data, but to obtain informative training data that broadens behavioral coverage across objects, scenes, and skills. Yet automatically curating task proposals to maximize the utility of collected data remains under-explored.

We introduce RoboGene, an agentic framework for generating diverse, informative manipulation tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile robots.

RoboGene combines （1） diversity-driven sampling for broad task coverage, （2） agentic self-reflection for task-quality assessment, and （3） human-verified feedback memory for execution-grounded validation and continual refinement.

Through quantitative analysis and large-scale real-world experiments, we collect 18k trajectories and introduce metrics for task feasibility and diversity. RoboGene significantly outperforms frontier foundation models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Pro.

VLA models trained on RoboGene-generated data achieve higher success rates and stronger generalization, highlighting the value of high-quality task generation. Project page: https://robogene-boost-vla.github.io/.

Datasets: Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/X-Humanoid/RoboGene) and ModelScope (https://modelscope.cn/datasets/X-Humanoid/RoboGene_tasks).

summary.en: RoboGene is an agentic framework for generating manipulation tasks for VLA pre-training across single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile robots. It combines diversity-driven sampling, agent self-reflection for task-quality assessment, and human-verified feedback memory for execution-grounded validation and refinement. The authors report collecting 18,000 trajectories through quantitative analysis and large-scale real-world experiments, and introduce task feasibility and diversity metrics. They say RoboGene outperforms models including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Pro, while VLA models trained on its generated data achieve higher success rates and stronger generalization.
summary.zh: 论文提出 RoboGene，一个为视觉—语言—动作预训练生成操作任务的智能体框架，覆盖单臂、双臂和移动机器人。框架结合多样性驱动采样、智能体自我反思评估任务质量，以及经人工验证的反馈记忆，用于基于执行情况验证和持续改进任务。作者报告，通过定量分析和大规模真实世界实验收集了 1.8 万条轨迹，并提出任务可行性与多样性指标；RoboGene 优于 GPT-4o、Gemini 2.5 Pro 等模型。用生成数据训练的模型表现出更高成功率和更强泛化能力。

sections.text:
Agile quadruped navigation in dynamic environments demands trajectories that are both dynamically feasible and provably collision-free.

Most real-time planners achieve tractability through a convex reduction that requires simplified kinematic models, discarding motion that the robot can readily execute, and certify safety only at discretization points, leaving open possible inter-sample collisions with moving obstacles.

We present a real-time motion planning framework that retains the fully-actuated $SE（2）$ model of a quadruped, with its anisotropic, heading-coupled velocity bounds, and accepts the resulting nonconvexity.

By parameterizing trajectories as composite Bernstein polynomials, we exploit the convex hull property to certify collision avoidance and the input bounds over the entirety of each planning horizon. Solved at online replanning rates, the optimization runs in closed loop, commanding body velocities to the locomotion controller.

We validate the approach in simulation against ablations and external baselines, and in hardware experiments on a quadruped navigating among unknown moving obstacles, recovering both lateral and heading-coupled motion that simplified models exclude.

summary.en: The paper presents a real-time planning framework for agile quadrupeds that retains a fully actuated SE(2) model with heading-coupled velocity bounds, accepting the resulting nonconvexity. Composite Bernstein polynomials use the convex hull property to certify collision avoidance and input bounds throughout each planning horizon. The optimization runs online in closed loop and sends body-velocity commands to the locomotion controller. The authors validate the method in simulation against ablations and external baselines, and in hardware experiments among unknown moving obstacles, demonstrating lateral and heading-coupled motions excluded by simplified models.
summary.zh: 论文提出面向敏捷四足机器人的实时运动规划框架，保留完整驱动的 SE(2) 模型及其方向相关速度限制，并接受由此产生的非凸优化问题。框架用复合 Bernstein 多项式参数化轨迹，利用凸包性质，在整个规划时域内验证碰撞规避和输入边界，而非仅检查离散时刻；优化在线闭环运行，并向运动控制器发送机身速度指令。作者在仿真中与消融及外部基线比较，并通过四足机器人硬件实验，在未知移动障碍物环境中验证方法，展示简化模型排除的侧向及方向耦合运动。

sections.text:
Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery.

We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration.

Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods.

The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies.

DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies.

Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies.

These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.

summary.en: The study combines whole-brain recordings in fruit flies with a neuromechanical digital twin to examine whether intrinsic goals can produce embodied agents that match fly behavior and representations of future voluntary action. A hierarchical policy selects from discrete motor primitives; agents are trained without external rewards using 20 intrinsic-motivation algorithms and evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay. The authors report that DIAYN performs best jointly on behavioral and neural prospective coding, captures individual differences in fly exploration, and reflects a biological interhemispheric kinematic encoding rule.
summary.zh: 研究结合果蝇全脑记录与神经力学数字孪生，考察内在目标能否使人工智能体在探索中呈现与果蝇相符的行为及未来自主行动表征。分层策略从离散运动原语中选择动作，研究者以 20 种好奇心、熵和能力类内在动机算法训练智能体，不使用外部奖励，并在虚拟系球实验中比较运动统计与神经表征。作者报告，DIAYN 在行为和神经前瞻编码方面综合表现最佳，其策略贴近个体果蝇探索差异，潜在活动也呈现生物果蝇的运动学半球间编码规则。结论来自该实验框架与比较。

sections.text:
World-action models (WAM) predict future states to guide robot actions, enabling learning from both action-free video and action-labeled interaction. Most inherit pretrained video generators, leaving WAM pretraining and scaling underexplored.

We introduce Genie Envisioner Act 2.0 (GE-Act 2.0), a world-action model whose trainable generative and action components are all initialized from scratch on manipulation data. It combines a control-oriented autoencoder (CoAE), a single-step visual planner (SVP), and an inverse dynamics model (IDM).

CoAE retains action- and instruction-relevant information under aggressive compression, while SVP produces a complete future state in one differentiable pass, so visual planning and inverse dynamics can be pretrained separately on complementary data.

The components are then jointly trained with knowledge-aligned selective optimization (KASO), which reduces mismatched supervision by selecting only predicted futures judged behaviorally compatible with the recorded action.

We evaluate pretrained checkpoints directly, without per-task fine-tuning, on 100 tasks across 20 manipulation skill groups with held-out scenes, backgrounds, lighting, and object instances.

Scaling co-training data from 300 to 30,000 hours raises success from 17.1% to 44.1% on G1-OP and from 13.4% to 31.1% on G2-90D; despite comprising less than 2% of the co-training data, G2-90D improves by 17.7 points, suggesting cross-embodiment transfer.

Gains span 19/20 and 18/20 skill groups, and skill-specific coverage strongly correlates with zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) success (Pearson r=0.80; Spearman rho=0.85).

Under the same protocol, the model grounds object, color, shape, and position references in at least 90% of trials and follows explicit instructions even when they conflict with an already-committed behavior or a conventional scene association.

summary.en: GE-Act 2.0 is a world-action model whose generative and action components are trained from scratch on manipulation data. It combines a control-oriented autoencoder, a single-step visual planner, and an inverse dynamics model. Selective optimization keeps predicted futures judged behaviorally compatible with recorded actions. The authors evaluate pretrained checkpoints without task-specific fine-tuning across 100 tasks and 20 skill groups, including held-out scenes and objects. They report improved success as co-training data scales, gains across most skill groups, correlation between skill coverage and zero-shot OOD success, and instruction grounding for object attributes and conflicting commands.
summary.zh: GE-Act 2.0是一种从零开始、以操作数据训练生成与动作组件的世界-动作模型，包含控制导向自编码器、单步视觉规划器和逆动力学模型。模型通过选择与记录动作在行为上相容的预测未来状态，减少不匹配监督。作者在20类技能、100项任务及未见场景等条件下直接评估预训练检查点，不做逐任务微调；报告称，共同训练数据从300小时扩至30,000小时后，两种机器人平台成功率均提升，且多数技能组有增益。技能覆盖与零样本分布外成功率相关，模型也能依据指令定位物体属性并处理与既有行为冲突的明确指令。

sections.text:
Robotics manipulation usually assumes that the shape and pose of the object are known to the robot prior to motion planning. However, precise geometric information is not always available in practice, and pose inference suffers from sensor uncertainties and view occlusion.

In this work, we propose a unified model-based geometric framework integrating robotic haptic perception, modeling, and manipulation planning.

Our novelties involve: \textit{i)} Introducing Bayesian Optimization (BO) to guide the haptic exploration for object shape inference, where superellipses are used to approximate geometric boundary; \textit{ii)} Adaptive formulation of manipulation potential encoding object geometry for quasi-static robot-object interaction; \textit{iii)} Proposing an online Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) for real-time pose inference based on model prediction and tactile feedback.

We deploy our system on a 2D robotic sorting task, and vary object geometries to validate the robustness and generalizability of our framework in both simulation and a real-world multi-arm setup.

summary.en: The paper presents a unified model-based geometric framework for robotic haptic perception, modeling, and manipulation planning, addressing unknown object geometry and uncertain, occluded pose observations. Bayesian optimization guides haptic exploration, with superellipses approximating object boundaries. An adaptive manipulation potential encodes geometry for quasi-static robot-object interaction, and an online ordinary differential equation combines model prediction with tactile feedback for real-time pose inference. The authors evaluate a 2D robotic sorting task with varied object geometries in simulation and a real-world multi-arm setup to assess robustness and generalizability.
summary.zh: 本文提出一个结合触觉感知、几何建模与操作规划的统一模型框架，用于物体形状估计和实时姿态推断。框架以贝叶斯优化引导触觉探索，并用超椭圆近似物体边界；自适应操作势能编码物体几何，以描述准静态机器人与物体的交互；在线常微分方程则结合模型预测和触觉反馈推断姿态。作者在二维机器人分拣任务中改变物体几何，在仿真和真实多臂设置中验证框架的鲁棒性与泛化性。摘要未给出具体性能数值。

sections.text:
Pure pursuit and its variants are widely used for mobile robot path tracking owing to their simplicity and computational efficiency.

However, many conventional approaches do not explicitly account for velocity and acceleration constraints, resulting in discrepancies between commanded and actual velocities that result in overshoot and degraded tracking performance.

To address this problem, this paper proposes dynamic window pure pursuit (DWPP), which fundamentally reformulates the command velocity computation process to explicitly incorporate velocity and acceleration constraints.

Specifically, DWPP formulates command velocity computation in the velocity space (the $v$-$\omega$ plane) and selects the command velocity as the point within the dynamic window that is closest to the line $\omega = \kappa v$.

Experimental results demonstrate that DWPP avoids constraint-violating commands and achieves superior path-tracking accuracy compared with conventional pure pursuit methods. The proposed method has been integrated into the official Nav2 repository and is publicly available (https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2).

summary.en: The paper proposes dynamic window pure pursuit (DWPP) for mobile-robot path tracking, addressing conventional methods that omit explicit velocity and acceleration constraints and may therefore overshoot. DWPP computes commands in velocity space, the v-ω plane, and selects the point within the dynamic window closest to the line ω = κv. Experimental results show that it avoids constraint-violating commands and tracks paths more accurately than conventional pure pursuit methods. The paper also states that DWPP has been integrated into the official Nav2 repository and is publicly available.

sections.text:
Language is a natural way to command robots, but converting a single instruction into a long-horizon, contact-rich hand-object interaction remains challenging: synthesized references are noisy, human-to-robot retargeting introduces embodiment bias, and fixed-reference tracking lets small errors snowball.

We address this with AdaDexTrack, a modulator-in-the-loop framework for language-conditioned manipulation tracking.

A distilled generalist tracker serves as the skill carrier, while a tightly aligned modulator performs three feedback corrections: reference modulation (continual adjustment of what to track), object-latent modulation (online adaptation of the object representation to recruit suitable skills), and positional-target modulation (small state-dependent refinements for execution).

The tracker is learned via large-scale specialist to generalist distillation on a corpus of language-conditioned hand-object trajectories; the modulator is trained with RL under the same task objective, ensuring tight coupling.

Across large-scale evaluations, AdaDexTrack consistently outperforms prior SOTA on unseen-trajectory and unseen-object sets in both average tracking error and success rate, demonstrating robustness and generalization.

We further show zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on real hardware, where adding the modulator yields substantial gains over a tracker-only variant.

AdaDexTrack reframes language-conditioned dexterous manipulation as modulated tracking, replacing the open-loop, fixed-reference tracking with in-loop modulation that adjusts the reference, object latent, and positional target, yielding drift-resistant execution from noisy text references.

summary.en: The paper presents AdaDexTrack, a framework for language-conditioned dexterous manipulation tracking. A distilled generalist tracker carries skills, while an in-loop modulator adjusts tracking references, object representations, and positional targets. The tracker is trained through specialist-to-generalist distillation, and the modulator through reinforcement learning. The authors report better average tracking error and success rate than prior methods on unseen-trajectory and unseen-object evaluations. They also report zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on real hardware, with the modulator outperforming a tracker-only variant.
summary.zh: 论文提出 AdaDexTrack，用于语言条件下的灵巧操作跟踪。框架以蒸馏得到的通用跟踪器为技能载体，并通过调制器在线调整跟踪参考、物体潜在表示和位置目标；跟踪器经专才到通才蒸馏训练，调制器用强化学习训练。作者称，大规模评测中，该方法在未见轨迹和未见物体集合上的平均跟踪误差与成功率优于既有方法；并报告了真实硬件上的零样本仿真到现实迁移，加入调制器优于仅使用跟踪器。

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited.

Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios.

To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components.

First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision.

Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. % This design introduces task-specific guidance while largely preserving the original VLA action-generation backbone.

In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning.

Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.

summary.en: The paper proposes CapPro, which adapts a vision-language-action policy to unseen manipulation tasks using a single human demonstration video, without target-task robot demonstrations or fine-tuning. A phase-aware module builds compact video and task-relevant query representations through visual token selection and phase-caption supervision. A video-conditioned module incorporates these representations into the pretrained policy’s action-conditioning context. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks reportedly show improved average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on source tasks.
summary.zh: 论文提出 CapPro，使视觉—语言—动作（VLA）策略仅凭一段人类示范视频适应未见操作任务，无需目标任务的机器人示范或微调。其阶段感知表示模块通过视觉词元选择和阶段字幕监督提取紧凑视频及任务相关查询表示；视频条件适配模块将这些表示纳入预训练 VLA 的动作条件上下文。作者称，跨源任务与未见目标任务的实验显示，CapPro 提升了未见目标任务组的平均表现，同时在源任务上保持相近表现。

sections.text:
Existing robot navigation methods primarily focus on isolated tasks, overlooking the need to accumulate knowledge and experience across repeated navigation episodes.

Although recent lifelong navigation methods have explored cross-task knowledge accumulation, they mainly focus on scene knowledge while neglecting historical navigation experience and its connection to scene evidence, limiting the ability to reflect on past mistakes and improve future decisions.

To address this limitation, this paper presents RetroNav, a training-free self-evolving navigation framework that integrates navigation, memory accumulation, and failure reflection.

Specifically, we develop a unified memory system that connects geometric and semantic scene knowledge with historical navigation experience, distinguishing objective observations from task-dependent interpretations. After each navigation attempt, an independent evaluator determines whether a retry is necessary.

If so, a Retrospection Agent revisits historical decisions using accumulated scene knowledge and navigation records, generating an evidence-grounded retry brief to guide the next attempt. RetroNav achieves state-of-the-art performance across five navigation benchmarks. Our method will be open-sourced at https://github.com/3dv-casia/RetroNav .

summary.en: The paper introduces RetroNav, a training-free framework for self-evolving navigation that combines navigation, memory accumulation, and failure reflection. Its unified memory connects geometric and semantic scene knowledge with historical navigation experience, distinguishing objective observations from task-dependent interpretations. After each attempt, an independent evaluator decides whether a retry is needed. If so, a Retrospection Agent reviews past decisions using accumulated scene knowledge and navigation records, then creates an evidence-grounded retry brief. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across five navigation benchmarks.
summary.zh: 论文提出 RetroNav，一个无需训练的自我演进导航框架，结合导航、记忆积累与失败反思。其统一记忆系统关联几何和语义场景知识与历史导航经验，并区分客观观察和依赖任务的解释。每次导航尝试后，独立评估器判断是否重试；若需要，回溯代理利用累积的场景知识和导航记录复查历史决策，生成基于证据的重试说明。作者报告，该方法在五个导航基准上达到最先进表现。

sections.text:
Latent world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time, so planning with them can degrade under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this degradation by updating the model during deployment.

Unlike pre-training on fixed data, TTA for planning is closed-loop: the planner uses model rollouts to select actions, and the resulting transitions drive the next update. This raises the question: which objective should guide TTA for planning?

Under a prediction-only objective, the model is fit only to the outcomes of its own actions, so it can remain wrong about the actions that would reach the goal, and low prediction error need not translate into better planning. Inspired by reward-biased maximum likelihood from adaptive control, we introduce Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA).

Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction.

Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points.

These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.

summary.en: The paper proposes Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA) to improve planning with latent world models under distribution shifts. Its objective minimizes both prediction loss on observed transitions and goal-reaching cost on the planner’s candidate rollouts, incorporating planning goals without additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts in manipulation, reaching, and navigation, the authors report average final planning success gains over a frozen model of 13.5 percentage points for OpTTA and 6.9 for the prediction-only AdaJEPA objective when adapting only the predictor. When adapting the encoder too, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. Experiments span three JEPA models and multiple planners.
summary.zh: 论文提出乐观测试时适配（OpTTA），用于改善分布变化下潜在世界模型的规划表现。其目标同时最小化已观察转移的预测损失，以及规划器候选轨迹的目标到达代价，使模型适配兼顾预测与规划目标，且不需额外环境交互。作者报告，在操作、到达和导航任务的视觉及环境变化实验中，仅适配预测器时，OpTTA 相对冻结模型平均提升最终规划成功率13.5个百分点，预测专用目标 AdaJEPA 提升6.9个百分点；同时适配编码器时分别提升13.5和7.5个百分点。实验涉及三种 JEPA 世界模型及不同规划器。

items.title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation

sections.text:
Running vision-language navigation fully onboard an aerial robot is hard, since grounding, planning, and control must share limited compute and a single-stage error is difficult to isolate in flight. End-to-end aerial policies fuse these stages into one network, giving up the observability and safety checks a modular stack keeps available.

We propose VLN on the Fly, an onboard stack that keeps grounding, planning, and control as separate, inspectable stages. A quantized VLM grounds an instruction to a coarse image cell, depth lifts it to a 3D goal, a fast B-spline planner returns a feasible trajectory, and a pretrained reinforcement learning policy tracks it to motor commands across quadrotors.

Across 15 onboard flights over three everyday referents in a controlled indoor volume, the stack reaches the target in 13 of 15 trials with 5.72 cm mean goal error and 39.3% average GPU utilization. In 6 additional cluttered-environment trials, the stack tracks collision-free trajectories under onboard perception gating.

summary.en: The paper presents VLN on the Fly, an onboard vision-language navigation stack that keeps grounding, planning, and control as inspectable stages. A quantized vision-language model maps instructions to coarse image regions; depth estimates a 3D goal, a B-spline planner produces a feasible trajectory, and a pretrained reinforcement learning policy tracks it to motor commands. In 15 onboard flights in a controlled indoor volume, the stack reached its target in 13 trials, with 5.72 cm mean goal error and 39.3% average GPU utilization. In six additional cluttered-environment trials, it tracked collision-free trajectories under onboard perception gating.
summary.zh: 本文提出“VLN on the Fly”机载视觉语言导航系统，将指令落地、规划和控制保留为可检查的独立阶段：量化视觉语言模型将指令映射到图像区域，深度信息将其转换为三维目标，快速B样条规划器生成可行轨迹，预训练强化学习策略负责跟踪并输出电机指令。在受控室内空间的15次机载飞行中，系统有13次到达目标，平均目标误差为5.72厘米，平均GPU利用率为39.3%。另有6次杂乱环境试验中，系统在机载感知门控下跟踪无碰撞轨迹。

sections.text:
World action models (WAMs) have emerged as an important class of generalist robot policies, aiming to transfer video prediction priors to action learning. However, we find that existing WAMs frequently produce incorrect motion predictions in open-ended environment, leading to erroneous actions.

We attribute this limitation to two factors: （1） base video models are not optimized for manipulation, and （2） naively incorporating action components into video models can substantially degrade their generalization capabilities.

We introduce Video Prediction Policy 2 (VPP2), a WAM that enables strong zero-shot generalization in both video prediction and action generation. First, we curate a large-scale, diverse dataset of manipulation videos to continue pretraining the base video foundation model.

We annotate video clips with detailed captions and perform \textit{event-level} video pretraining to promote generalization across open-ended manipulation tasks. Second, we post-train and distill the video model into a single-step visual planner with fixed prediction horizon.

Finally, we introduce action module via a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture to learn implicit inverse dynamics model.

Experiments demonstrate three key results: （1） VPP2-14B outperforms Cosmos3-64B by 11.0\% points in video prediction instruction-following success rate on open-ended tasks; （2） VPP2 surpasses the strongest baseline by 18.5\% points in success rate on real-world zero-shot ALOHA manipulation tasks; and （3） following benchmark-specific post-training, VPP2 achieves the highest success rates among evaluated methods on the challenging LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-OOD, and RoboDojo benchmarks.

summary.en: The paper introduces Video Prediction Policy 2 (VPP2), addressing incorrect motion predictions by world action models in open-ended environments. The authors attribute the issue to base video models not being optimized for manipulation and to action components that may harm generalization. VPP2 continues pretraining on diverse manipulation videos with detailed captions and event-level training, then post-trains and distills the model into a single-step visual planner with a fixed horizon. A mixture-of-transformers action module learns implicit inverse dynamics. Experiments report gains in open-task video prediction instruction following, real-world zero-shot ALOHA manipulation, and several benchmarks after benchmark-specific post-training.
summary.zh: 本文提出视频预测策略VPP2，针对世界动作模型在开放环境中运动预测错误的问题，指出基础视频模型未针对操作任务优化，直接加入动作成分也可能损害泛化。作者使用多样化操作视频继续预训练基础模型，以细致描述和事件级训练促进开放任务泛化，再将模型后训练并蒸馏为固定预测时域的单步视觉规划器，并通过混合变换器架构学习隐式逆动力学。实验报告称，VPP2在开放任务视频预测指令遵循、真实世界零样本ALOHA操作，以及经特定基准后训练的多个基准上优于所比较方法。

sections.text:
World Action Models (WAMs) combine future-video prediction with robot action learning, yet improvements in task success alone do not reveal how predictive supervision manifests in execution behavior or whether its benefits persist under task and environmental shifts.

We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family. Under clean conditions on seen tasks, predictive supervision increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points, respectively.

Trajectory clustering further reveals higher success rates within several coarse trajectory clusters, including cases where cluster frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in changes in the prevalence of trajectory patterns.

However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision.

We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for $\pi_{0.5}$, where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%.

These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting.

summary.en: The paper studies future-video prediction as supervision for robot action learning through controlled loss ablations in FastWAM and OpenWAM. On seen tasks under clean conditions, predictive supervision raises success rates, with trajectory analyses showing gains within several clusters. The benefits transfer inconsistently to unseen tasks and do not provide a consistent advantage under the evaluated environmental randomizations. The authors also report improved success for π0.5 when a lightweight Transformer predictor is used as an auxiliary training objective.
summary.zh: 论文通过在 FastWAM 和 OpenWAM 中控制未来视频预测损失消融，考察预测监督如何影响机器人动作执行及其在任务和环境变化下的表现。在已见任务的干净条件下，两种模型的成功率均有提升，轨迹聚类也显示若干类别内成功率提高；但未见任务上的收益因模型和任务而异，在所评估的环境随机化下，两者成功率较低，且预测监督没有稳定优势。作者还报告，将轻量 Transformer 预测器作为训练期辅助目标用于 π0.5，成功率有所提升。

sections.text:
Long-horizon embodied navigation may be interrupted by a higher-priority instruction before the current task sequence is complete. The agent must finish its current atomic task, execute the inserted task, and resume the remaining sequence from the updated environment state, where its viewpoint and available navigation candidates may have changed.

To evaluate this capability, we introduce PIFR benchmark, a novel task for runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. PIFR includes single, repeated, and nested interruption settings,with stage-specific metrics for inserted-task completion, resumption of the original task, and completion of the full sequence.

Evaluations show that recovery performance varies across interruption conditions, while aggregate success can obscure differences in interruption handling and resumption. We further propose a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline to improve target re-grounding after interruption.

Together, PIFR and the baseline provide a systematic framework for studying interruption handling and task recovery in long-horizon embodied navigation.

summary.en: The paper introduces PIFR, a benchmark for evaluating whether embodied navigation agents can handle a higher-priority task inserted into a long task sequence and then resume the original sequence. It covers single, repeated, and nested interruptions, with separate metrics for inserted-task completion, resumption, and full-sequence completion. Evaluations show that recovery varies across interruption conditions and that aggregate success can conceal these differences. The authors also propose a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline for re-grounding targets after interruption.
summary.zh: 论文提出 PIFR 基准，用于评估具身导航中执行长序列任务时遭遇高优先级指令打断后，完成插入任务并恢复原序列的能力。基准涵盖单次、重复和嵌套打断，并分别衡量插入任务完成、原任务恢复和完整序列完成。评估显示，不同打断条件下的恢复表现有所差异，整体成功率可能掩盖处理打断及恢复任务的差别。作者还提出轻量级候选目标排序基线，以改善打断后的目标重新定位。

sections.text:
Robots that follow natural-language instructions unlock a wide range of autonomous applications in households, warehouses, and labs. Real-world environments are diverse and often heavily cluttered, requiring robots to plan over multiple steps, act, and replan as they work toward a goal.

We present CLARO (CLutter-Aware Robot Orchestrator), a VLM agent that orchestrates a set of perception and manipulation skills: open-vocabulary object detection, segmentation, 6-DoF grasping, and non-prehensile pushing to locate and retrieve a language-specified target in clutter.

CLARO maintains a memory of its past actions to support long-horizon execution, and emits manipulation targets (grasp poses/3D waypoints) allowing transfer across robot arms without task-specific training.

We evaluate CLARO against a range of methods on a dynamic simulation environment and standard image-based benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization across object classes, lighting, and clutter levels. CLARO attains an average success rate of 89.1%, a relative improvement of over 16% on the strongest competing method in high cluttered scenes.

We further analyze performance along grounding and grasping axes to characterize where each method succeeds and fails. Finally, we deploy CLARO on a robot arm across diverse cluttered scenes, achieving a success rate of 88.8%, and demonstrating strong sim2real generalizability.

summary.en: The paper presents CLARO, a vision-language-model agent that coordinates perception and manipulation skills to find and retrieve language-specified objects in clutter. It combines open-vocabulary detection, segmentation, six-degree-of-freedom grasping, and pushing, while using action history to support long-horizon execution. Its grasp poses and 3D waypoints are intended to transfer across robot arms without task-specific training. The authors report evaluations in dynamic simulation, image-based benchmarks, and deployments on a robot arm across cluttered scenes.
summary.zh: 论文介绍 CLARO，一种使用视觉语言模型代理协调感知与操作技能的机器人系统，可在杂乱环境中根据语言指令定位并取回目标物体。系统组合开放词汇检测、分割、六自由度抓取和推挤，并利用过去动作记忆支持长时执行；输出抓取姿态或三维路点，以支持跨机械臂迁移。作者报告，CLARO 在动态仿真和图像基准上对物体类别、光照及杂乱程度具有较强泛化表现，并在真实机械臂的多种杂乱场景中进行了部署评估。

items.title: CLARO: Clutter Aware Robot Orchestrator for Open-Vocabulary Grasping using VLM Agents
